caption: All blue arrows have the same direction and length. On the polar grid, the red radial and gold angular contributions change as their local directions turn.
alt: The same two rightward blue arrows on Cartesian and polar grids. Their radial and angular decompositions differ on the polar grid.

caption: A spatial cross-section of a released cloud outside a spherical mass. Gold arrows show acceleration relative to the freely falling centre; blue dots show an exaggerated short-time deformation. The common inward fall is absent from this comoving picture.
alt: Two views of a small particle cloud. Initially circular with zero relative velocity, it later stretches radially and squeezes transversely. Gold arrows on the initial cloud show relative acceleration.

caption: The green route A–N–B–A bounds a spherical octant. Blue arrows follow parallel transport; at A the returned arrow is gold. The inset compares the start and return in A’s tangent plane: their true angle is 90°, although the sphere’s perspective view skews drawn angles. Arrow lengths in the perspective drawing are schematic.
alt: A sphere with a triangular route from equatorial A to the north pole N, down to equatorial B and back to A. Blue arrows are transported along the legs. At A a gold returned arrow is perpendicular to the initial one, shown without perspective in a tangent-plane inset.

caption: Two illustrative diagonal relative-acceleration maps in a local freely falling spatial frame. The right-hand map stretches one axis and squeezes two, giving zero trace despite nonzero tides. Arrows and numbers show instantaneous acceleration coefficients in common arbitrary units, not finite particle displacements. Later volume evolution also depends on the cloud’s expansion, shear and rotation.
alt: Two columns compare relative accelerations along x, y and z. Uniform inward arrows have coefficients minus one on every axis and trace minus three. Radial outward arrows with coefficient plus two and transverse inward arrows with minus one give a trace of zero.

caption: The green strip is an imaginary internal face, not a wall. Equal right-going and left-going populations have opposite momentum densities but positive diagonal momentum flux from both streams. Here qₓ is a particle’s momentum component and vₓ its velocity component. This one-axis sketch illustrates one stress component; a perfect fluid has isotropic stress in all three spatial directions.
alt: Blue particles carry positive momentum rightward across a marked internal face. Gold particles carry negative momentum leftward across the same face. Their bulk momentum cancels, while the product of momentum and velocity is positive in both streams.

caption: Each vertical line is a stationary clock’s history; upward is a common static coordinate time. Gold lines connect successive emissions with receptions after the same coordinate-time delay. Blue marks are proper-time ticks, more closely spaced on the higher clock. The rate difference is deliberately exaggerated; the diagram is schematic and does not specify the local slope or speed of the light paths.
alt: Three light pulses connect a lower stationary emitter with a higher stationary receiver. Equal coordinate-time spacing is preserved, while the same two pulse intervals span four emitter tick units and six receiver tick units in an exaggerated illustration.

caption: Local radial future cones in the Schwarzschild black-hole region and exterior, drawn in horizon-penetrating coordinates T=v−r with c=1. The outgoing boundary points outward at r=4m, stays at r=2m on the future horizon, and points inward at r=m. The ingoing boundary points inward throughout. These are local tangent directions, not finite light-ray trajectories; cone slopes are coordinate-dependent and each local observer still measures light speed c.
alt: Three local future light cones in regular Schwarzschild coordinates. Outside the horizon one boundary points towards increasing radius. At the horizon it is vertical along the boundary. Inside, both future null boundaries point towards smaller radius.
